analysis.one_liner: Taxes fund managers' performance profits as ordinary income instead of the lower capital-gains rate.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 13 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a markup, a vote, or floor action before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Fund managers at private equity, hedge fund, and venture capital firms often take a share of their investors' profits — called carried interest — and pay tax on it at the low long-term capital-gains rate (up to about 20%) instead of the higher rate that applies to salaries. This bill would tax that performance income as ordinary income, treat gains from selling the interest itself as ordinary income, subject it to self-employment taxes, and raise the penalty for underpaying taxes on it. Genuine capital investors' money is exempted, and family-run investment partnerships get special treatment.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, because fund managers would pay tax on performance income at the same rates workers pay on wages, narrowing a tax preference available almost exclusively to the highest-earning investors and raising federal revenue.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary taxpayers and the federal treasury

how_it_helps.text: The bill recharacterizes the net capital gain allocated to an 'investment services partnership interest' — a fund manager's carried interest — as ordinary income, except for gains attributable to genuine invested capital [S2][S3].

It also counts investment services partnership income in net earnings from self-employment, so managers pay self-employment (Social Security and Medicare) taxes on it, and raises the underpayment penalty from 20% to 40% for attempts to avoid the rules [S2][S3].

Capital actually contributed by the manager ('qualified capital interests') keeps capital-gains treatment, and certain family partnerships are exempted, so the bill targets service-based performance pay rather than investment returns generally [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Managers at private equity, hedge fund, venture capital, and real estate investment partnerships, whose performance-based income would be taxed at ordinary-income rates (up to 37%) plus self-employment taxes, and whose firms would face new valuation and recordkeeping rules; some of that cost could be passed to fund investors through higher fees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity and hedge fund managers

drawbacks.text: Opponents have long argued that taxing carried interest as ordinary income would discourage risk-taking and make it harder to form investment partnerships that channel capital into companies, real estate, and startups — a trade-off an honest supporter should acknowledge, though the bill preserves capital-gains treatment for managers' own invested money.

The bill is technically intricate: distinguishing a manager's service-based share from genuine invested capital requires extensive valuation, allocation, and recordkeeping rules, which would add compliance costs and disputes [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is straightforward fairness in tax rates — paying for services with your share of profits is taxed like pay for services, while your own invested capital keeps its break. The compliance complexity is real and the revenue effect depends on how fund structures respond, but the cost of the preference is concentrated among a small group of very high earners while the benefit is spread across all taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it — no markup, no vote, no floor debate — before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Sen. Tammy Baldwin introduced the Carried Interest Fairness Act of 2017 on May 3, 2017, joined by 13 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans [S1][S4].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance; that referral was the final entry in its action history [S5].
With the 115th Congress ending on January 3, 2019, the bill died in committee without ever reaching the Senate floor [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fund managers at private equity, hedge fund, and venture capital firms, who kept the lower capital-gains rate on performance income because the bill never received a committee vote or floor action.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fund managers keeping the capital-gains break

for.name: Sen. Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the Senate.

for.name: 13 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action — no markup or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As chairman, never scheduled a markup or consideration of the bill during the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 senators associated with the bill were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored it, and the Republican-controlled Finance Committee and Senate never acted on it.

industries.industry: Private equity and hedge fund managers
industries.note: Their signature compensation — the carried interest — would be taxed at ordinary-income rates plus self-employment tax, ending a break that lets highly paid managers pay a lower rate than wage earners. The industry's interest in keeping the break runs against ordinary taxpayers who would otherwise shoulder more of the tax load.

industries.industry: Venture capital and real estate partnership managers
industries.note: Real estate held for rental or investment counts as a specified asset, so real estate and venture partnerships' carried interests would be covered, though certain family real estate partnerships and REIT-linked structures are carved out. Fund investors could ultimately bear some of the added tax and compliance cost through fees.

industries.industry: Accounting, tax advisory, and fund administration services
industries.note: The bill requires new reporting, recordkeeping, and valuation guidance, creating compliance work for tax professionals — routine fallout of any tax-rule change.
